blocks.text: A 34-year-old woman presents to the gynaecology clinic because she has been trying to conceive for two years. She has one child from a previous pregnancy five years ago.

items.text: Take a focused history.
Identify possible causes of secondary infertility.
Outline appropriate investigations.
Explain management options to the patient.

blocks.text: Alternative scenarios

items.text: A woman who previously delivered by caesarean section and has not conceived again.
A woman with a previous ectopic pregnancy and subsequent difficulty conceiving.
A woman who had a miscarriage followed by uterine evacuation and now has scanty menstruation.
A couple with a previous child together but current abnormal semen analysis.

blocks.text: Secondary infertility is the inability to achieve a pregnancy after a specified period of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse in a person who has previously achieved a pregnancy.

items.text: 12 months of trying if the female partner is younger than 35 years.
6 months if the female partner is aged 35 years or older.
Earlier if there are risk factors, such as irregular or absent menstruation, previous ectopic pregnancy, suspected tubal disease or known male-factor infertility.

blocks.text: Do not confuse secondary infertility with secondary amenorrhoea. Secondary infertility concerns difficulty achieving another pregnancy; secondary amenorrhoea means menstruation has stopped after previously occurring.

rows: Previous pregnancy, miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy or delivery
Ovulatory, tubal, uterine, male or combined factors
The same causes, including newly acquired problems
What may have changed since the previous pregnancy?

blocks.text: OSCE pearl: A previous pregnancy does not prove that current fertility is normal. Fertility can change because of age, infection, surgery, endocrine disease or changes in sperm quality.
Begin with a professional, empathetic approach.

items.text: Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Confirm the patient's identity.
Ensure privacy and obtain consent.
Acknowledge the previous pregnancy without making assumptions about the outcome.
Explain that you will ask about both partners and any changes since the previous conception.
Ask whether the patient wishes to have her partner present.
Use non-judgmental language and offer emotional support.

blocks.text: “Hello, my name is …, and I am one of the doctors in the gynaecology clinic. I understand that you have conceived before but are now finding it difficult to become pregnant again. I appreciate that this may be frustrating or distressing. I would like to ask about your previous pregnancy, menstrual cycles, any illnesses or procedures since then, and your partner's reproductive health. This will help us identify possible causes and decide on appropriate investigations. Is that alright with you?”
The most important difference from primary infertility is that you must establish the details of the previous pregnancy and look for events or conditions that may have affected fertility afterward.

content_groups.group_title: A. History of the presenting complaint

items.text: How long have you been trying to conceive again?
When did you stop contraception?
How frequently do you have sexual intercourse?
Have you had any positive pregnancy tests since the previous pregnancy?
Has either partner previously undergone fertility investigations?
Has anything changed in your menstrual cycle or general health since the previous pregnancy?
Has your partner fathered any pregnancies with another partner since then, if relevant and appropriate to ask?

blocks.text: Interpret the answers in the context of the couple's age, duration of attempts and previous reproductive history.
This is a high-yield section.

items.text: How many times have you been pregnant?
What were the outcomes of each pregnancy?
Were there any miscarriages, ectopic pregnancies or terminations?
Did you deliver vaginally or by caesarean section?
Were there complications such as postpartum haemorrhage, retained placenta, puerperal sepsis or uterine infection?
Did you undergo dilatation and curettage or another uterine procedure?
Were there complications involving the placenta or uterus?
Did you breastfeed, and have your menstrual cycles returned to their previous pattern?

blocks.text: **Why these questions matter**
Previous ectopic pregnancy

Raises concern for tubal damage, particularly if the tube was removed or the patient has a history of pelvic infection. Establish the treatment received and whether the contralateral tube was assessed.
Miscarriage followed by uterine evacuation
Intrauterine adhesions may develop after uterine instrumentation, especially when followed by scanty menstruation or amenorrhoea.
Previous caesarean section
Consider uterine scar-related pathology, adhesions or a caesarean scar defect when supported by symptoms or imaging. A previous caesarean section does not automatically explain infertility.
Previous puerperal or pelvic infection
May result in tubal damage or pelvic adhesions, depending on the site and severity of infection.

items.text: Pelvic inflammatory disease or sexually transmitted infections.
Ectopic pregnancy.

blocks.text: Clinical reasoning: A woman who conceived previously but subsequently developed PID may now have tubal-factor infertility. Previous fertility does not exclude acquired tubal obstruction.

blocks.text: For example, a woman who previously had regular cycles and now has amenorrhoea with hot flushes requires assessment for ovarian insufficiency and other causes of amenorrhoea.

content_groups.group_title: H. Lifestyle, family and psychosocial history

blocks.text: Explore weight, nutrition, smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs, occupational exposures, medication use, relationship stress and the emotional impact of infertility.
Ask about the couple's expectations and whether there are financial, cultural or religious concerns that may influence their preferred treatment.
In a history-only station, explain what you would examine. In a combined station, obtain consent and use a chaperone for intimate examinations according to local practice.

blocks.text: Scenario 1: Previous ectopic pregnancy

“This is a 32-year-old woman presenting with secondary infertility following a previous ectopic pregnancy. Acquired tubal-factor infertility is a concern. I would review her previous treatment and tubal status, arrange appropriate assessment of tubal patency, obtain semen analysis and evaluate ovulatory function as indicated.”
Scenario 2: Previous uterine evacuation

“This is a woman with secondary infertility and markedly reduced menstrual flow following uterine evacuation. Intrauterine adhesions are a differential diagnosis. I would arrange pelvic ultrasound and, if indicated, saline infusion sonography or hysteroscopy to assess the uterine cavity.”
Scenario 3: New irregular menstruation

“This woman has secondary infertility associated with newly irregular menstrual cycles. Ovulatory dysfunction is suspected. I would assess for PCOS and other endocrine causes, evaluate her partner with semen analysis and assess tubal patency according to her history.”
Remember the same broad categories as in primary infertility, but pay particular attention to acquired causes.

items.text: Tubal-factor infertility: PID, previous ectopic pregnancy, pelvic surgery or adhesions.
Ovulatory dysfunction: PCOS, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia or primary ovarian insufficiency.
Uterine-factor infertility: Intrauterine adhesions, cavity-distorting fibroids, endometrial polyps or selected scar-related pathology.
Male-factor infertility: New testicular disease, medication effects, obstruction or abnormal semen parameters.
Endometriosis: Especially with dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia or chronic pelvic pain.
Age-related decline in fertility: Particularly relevant when there has been a long interval since the previous pregnancy.
Unexplained infertility: Consider only after an appropriate evaluation has not identified a cause.

blocks.text: Investigate both partners in parallel, with particular attention to events since the previous pregnancy.

rows: Confirm recent ovulation when needed; time according to the expected next period
Consider in amenorrhoea or suspected ovarian insufficiency
Help assess ovarian reserve and plan fertility treatment when relevant
Assess uterus, endometrium, ovaries and adnexa
Consider for selected cases of suspected pelvic disease or when surgery is otherwise indicated

blocks.text: Before procedures involving the uterine cavity or fallopian tubes, exclude pregnancy and assess for active infection according to local protocols.

items.text: Semen analysis.
Repeat semen analysis if indicated.
Focused male reproductive examination when appropriate.
Hormonal testing for selected abnormalities.
Further imaging or genetic testing where clinically indicated.

blocks.text: If a woman has a previous ectopic pregnancy, HSG may help assess tubal patency, but the findings must be interpreted in context. Apparent tubal occlusion, particularly proximal occlusion, may occasionally be due to spasm or technical factors and may require further assessment.
Management depends on the cause, age, duration of infertility, ovarian reserve where relevant, tubal status, semen findings and the couple's preferences.
Acknowledge the distress and explain that a previous pregnancy does not guarantee future fertility. Discuss the findings without assigning blame.

items.text: Encourage regular intercourse every 2–3 days.
Review medications and chronic medical conditions.
Encourage smoking cessation and avoidance of recreational drugs.
Promote balanced nutrition and a healthy weight.
Recommend folic acid, generally 400 micrograms daily for women at usual risk, with higher doses for specific indications.
Provide counselling and emotional support where helpful.

blocks.text: Ovulatory dysfunction
Treat the underlying disorder. Letrozole is generally first-line for appropriate patients with PCOS-related anovulatory infertility when no other infertility factor has been identified.
Tubal-factor infertility
Assess the site and severity of disease. Selected patients may benefit from surgery, while significant bilateral tubal disease often favours IVF.
Intrauterine adhesions
Refer for specialist assessment. Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis may be considered when adhesions are confirmed and treatment is appropriate.
Male-factor infertility
Investigate and treat reversible causes where possible. Options may include selected surgery, IUI, IVF or ICSI depending on the semen findings and the couple's circumstances.
Unexplained infertility
Discuss expectant management in selected couples, ovarian stimulation with IUI where appropriate, or IVF depending on age, duration of infertility, previous treatment and local guidance.

Refer early for specialist fertility assessment when there is advanced reproductive age, previous ectopic pregnancy with suspected tubal disease, amenorrhoea, suspected ovarian insufficiency, severe male-factor infertility or prolonged infertility.
Do not delay assessment simply because the couple has conceived before.
Review investigation results with both partners where appropriate, agree on the next steps, and provide realistic counselling about prognosis, treatment choices, costs and possible risks.
Q1. What is secondary infertility?
Answer: Failure to achieve a pregnancy after an appropriate period of regular unprotected intercourse in someone who has previously achieved a pregnancy.
Q2. What is the most important difference between taking a history for primary and secondary infertility?

Answer: In secondary infertility, I would obtain a detailed history of previous pregnancies and look for acquired problems such as ectopic pregnancy, PID, uterine instrumentation, pelvic surgery and age-related decline.
Q3. How can a previous ectopic pregnancy cause infertility?

Answer: The ectopic pregnancy may reflect pre-existing tubal damage, and treatment may involve removal or damage of a fallopian tube. The remaining tube's patency and the overall tubal history need assessment.
Q4. What is Asherman syndrome?

Answer: Intrauterine adhesions that may partially or completely obliterate the uterine cavity, often following uterine instrumentation or pregnancy-related complications. Patients may present with scanty menstruation, amenorrhoea, infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss.
Q5. Does having a previous child exclude male-factor infertility?
Answer: No. Male reproductive function can change over time, and a previous pregnancy does not exclude current male-factor infertility. Semen analysis remains an important initial investigation.
Q6. How would you investigate a woman with secondary infertility and regular cycles?
Answer: Take a full history, assess the male partner with semen analysis, evaluate tubal patency and pelvic anatomy, and assess ovulation or ovarian reserve when indicated by the clinical context.
Q7. What is the significance of age in secondary infertility?
Answer: Oocyte quantity and quality decline with age, affecting the likelihood of conception and increasing miscarriage risk. Age influences how urgently investigations and treatment should proceed.
Q8. What are the indications for IVF in secondary infertility?

Answer: Possible indications include significant bilateral tubal disease, selected cases of severe male-factor infertility, some cases of reduced reproductive potential and failure of appropriate initial treatment. The decision depends on the individual assessment.

items.text: Assuming that previous conception proves normal current fertility.
Failing to ask about ectopic pregnancy and its treatment.
Overlooking uterine instrumentation after miscarriage.
Attributing all infertility following caesarean delivery to the uterine scar.
Investigating the woman without evaluating the male partner.
Ordering tests without considering the patient's age, history and symptoms.
Failing to address the emotional impact of infertility.
Promising that a specific treatment will result in pregnancy.

blocks.title: Use this to remember key elements of the previous pregnancy history:

items.text: P — Previous pregnancy outcomes.
R — Retained placenta, postpartum haemorrhage or puerperal infection.
E — Ectopic pregnancy.
G — Gynaecological or uterine procedures.
N — Number of pregnancies and their outcomes.
A — Abdominal or pelvic surgery.
N — New menstrual changes.
C — Caesarean section or other complications.
Y — Your partner's current reproductive health.

blocks.title: Before leaving the station, ensure that you have:

items.text: Established the duration of infertility.
Documented the previous pregnancy and its outcome.
Asked about changes in menstrual cycles.
Screened for PID, ectopic pregnancy, uterine procedures and pelvic surgery.
Assessed both partners.
Explained appropriate investigations.
Discussed cause-specific management and referral.
Addressed the couple's emotional needs.

blocks.text: The key takeaway: In secondary infertility, ask not only why pregnancy is not occurring now, but also what may have changed since the previous pregnancy.
